title: The President's Formal Powers
short: The Constitution makes the President commander in chief and gives the powers to veto, to pardon, to make treaties and appoint officers with the Senate's consent, to receive ambassadors and to give Congress information on the State of the Union.
trouble: Students think a presidential pardon can cover state crimes. The pardon power covers only federal offenses.

blocks.html: The President's formal (constitutional) powers are the ones written in Article II and in Article I's veto clause. A President who meets the qualifications takes an oath to "preserve, protect and defend the Constitution" and gets these tools.

blocks.html: Article II gives the President fewer listed powers than Article I gives Congress, and most come with a partner or a check. Hamilton argued in Federalist No. 69 that the President's powers were far smaller than a king's: the king could declare war and make treaties alone, and his veto was absolute. The pardon is the great exception: it needs no one's consent. Hamilton defended it in Federalist No. 74 as a way to temper justice with mercy and, in a rebellion, to offer peace. It can come before charges are filed (President Ford pardoned Richard Nixon in 1974 before any charge), but it reaches only federal offenses.

The Constitution makes the President commander in chief and gives the powers to veto, to pardon (federal offenses), to make treaties and appoint officers with the Senate's consent, to receive ambassadors, and to report on the State of the Union.

blocks.title: Can the President pardon this?
blocks.q: A person is convicted of a state crime in a state court. Can the President pardon her?
steps: The pardon power covers "Offences against the United States": federal crimes.
A state crime is pardoned (if at all) by the state's governor or pardon board.

blocks.title: Formal or not?
blocks.q: Is giving the State of the Union address in person before Congress a formal power?
steps: Article II, Section 3 requires the President to "give to the Congress Information of the State of the Union."
It does not say how. Washington and Adams spoke in person; Jefferson sent written messages; Woodrow Wilson revived the speech in 1913.
blocks.a: The duty to inform is formal; the speech in person is a custom.

blocks.html: Thinking a presidential pardon can cover state crimes. The pardon power covers only federal offenses, and never impeachment. Check: ask who prosecuted the crime: the United States, or a state?
